# Four Hundredfold

The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon. It is also, by a coincidence that has no right to exist, about four hundred times farther away. Divide one by the other and the numbers cancel—which is why, every year or two, somewhere on Earth, the Moon slides in front of the Sun and covers it almost perfectly: a coin eclipsing a coin, a dinner plate blotting out a dinner plate. The match is never exact. The Moon's orbit is elliptical, its distance wavering, so sometimes the cover comes up small and leaves a blazing ring—an annular eclipse, the "ring of fire." But close enough, often enough, that for a few minutes over certain patches of the planet, day turns to night in the middle of the afternoon.

Nothing in physics requires this. Elsewhere in the solar system, moons eclipse the Sun by accident of scale—enormous overshoots, or puny transits like Phobos crossing the Martian sun—but the near-perfect match occurs nowhere else we know of. It is ours alone, and it is on loan. Laser ranging, pulses bounced off reflectors the Apollo astronauts left on the lunar surface, shows the Moon drifting away at about 3.8 centimeters per year. Too slow to notice, fast enough to matter over geological time. The coincidence is decaying. In a few hundred million years the match will fail for good, and total eclipses will simply be over. We live in the narrow window when the geometry works. Everyone who has ever stood in the Moon's shadow lived inside the same few hundred million years—a rounding error in the life of the Earth.

The strange thing about totality, the thing no one adequately warns you about, is that it's binary. A 99 percent eclipse is daylight. The Sun pours out so much light that even a sliver keeps the world ordinary; you need a proper filter even to see that something is wrong. Then the last sliver goes, and the switch flips. Venus appears. The horizon turns sunset-colored in every direction at once—the light of all the places outside the shadow, leaking in. The temperature drops several degrees. Birds, by many reports, go quiet and head for their roosts. And overhead, where the Sun should be, there is a black hole in the sky wreathed in white silk: the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, always there and never seen, drowned all its life by the surface it surrounds. The shadow itself races across the land at thousands of kilometers per hour, faster than sound. Totality lasts minutes. People scream. Annie Dillard, writing of the 1979 eclipse, compared a partial eclipse to a total one as kissing a man is to marrying him—and she offered the screaming, the weeping, as evidence, not decoration.

I have never stood in one myself. I know totality the way almost everyone does, by report—but the reports have a peculiar quality: they converge. That does not happen with roller coasters.

We have known how to anticipate the thing for a very long time. Babylonian astronomers, with no idea of orbits, ground out predictions from the Saros cycle—eighteen years, eleven days, eight hours—and handed the arithmetic down for generations. Herodotus tells of an eclipse Thales forecast that interrupted a battle between the Lydians and the Medes in 585 BCE; the soldiers, taking the darkened sky as an omen, negotiated peace on the spot. Embellished, probably. But an eclipse recorded in Assyria in 763 BCE still anchors the chronology of the ancient Near East; historians string their dates from it like laundry from a line.

Eclipses kept paying out. In 1868, astronomers pointed a spectroscope at the flame-colored prominences visible during totality and found a line matching no element on Earth. They named it helium, for Helios, and it took nearly thirty years to find any here—an element discovered in the Sun before it was found in the ground. In 1919, Arthur Eddington photographed the stars near the darkened Sun and found them shifted by the amounts general relativity demanded; Einstein woke up famous. And the corona itself is still keeping secrets. Its thin gas runs at over a million degrees, hundreds of times hotter than the surface below it—a paradox without a complete solution, and a reason scientists still chase the shadow even though coronagraphs can fake the event. The fakes are good. The innermost corona still belongs to the Moon.

Which points at the almost philosophical thing. We know everything about eclipses—the geometry, the physics, the timing to the second—and yet people who know all of it, professional astronomers, veterans of a dozen shadows, report being flattened anyway. Philosophers have a thought experiment about a woman raised in a black-and-white room who masters the physics of color; when she steps out and sees red for the first time, does she learn anything new? Totality is the strongest real-world case for yes. The facts compress almost none of the experience. Most knowledge travels well: read about Paris and you come away with a fraction of Paris. Totality doesn't divide. It's digital. Either the Sun is covered or it isn't; either you were there or you weren't.

And the whole apparatus is temporary. The Moon recedes, the match will fail, and some afternoon a few hundred million years from now there will be a last total eclipse of the Sun. No one will know to mark it. It will look like all the eclipses around it in the record—a ring of fire, lovely, unremarkable. The most reliably astonishing sight nature affords is a loan whose repayment date appears in no ledger. That may be the lesson, if eclipses carry one: the window is always narrow, the geometry always temporary, and the right response to a few minutes of impossible shadow is the same as the response to anything that happens only now—be there, or wish you had been.
